docs.title: ifctrano
docs.text: ifctrano

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: ifctrano is yet another IFC to energy simulation tool designed to translate Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) models into energy simulation models in Modelica.

docs.title: Key Differentiator
docs.text: Unlike most translation approaches that rely on space boundaries (IfcRelSpaceBoundary), ifctrano operates solely on geometrical representation. This is crucial because space boundaries are rarely available in IFC models. Instead, ifctrano requires at least the definition of IfcSpace objects to build energy simulation models.

docs.title: Space-Zone Mapping
docs.text: For now, each space is considered as a single thermal zone, and the necessary space boundaries are automatically generated.

docs.title: Why ifctrano?
docs.text:
✅ No reliance on IfcRelSpaceBoundary

✅ Works with geometric representation only

✅ Supports Modelica-based energy simulation

✅ Tested on multiple open-source IFC files

docs.title: Research & Background
docs.text: ifctrano is inspired by existing research, including this journal paper: Automated Translation of IFC to Energy Models. However, it takes a more robust and practical approach that doesn’t require explicit space boundaries.

docs.title: Open Source IFC Test Files
docs.text:
ifctrano has been tested using open-source IFC files from various repositories:

  • 🐋 BIM Whale IFC Samples
  • 🏗️ IfcSampleFiles
  • 🎭 BIM2Modelica
  • 🕸️ Ifc2Graph Test Files
  • 🔓 Open Source BIM

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
See the installation page, then the tutorials. How ifctrano works explains the translation and the generated models.

💡 ifctrano aims to make energy simulation model generation from IFC files simpler, more accessible, and less reliant on incomplete IFC attributes. 🚀

docs.title: How ifctrano works
docs.text: ifctrano reads the geometry of an IFC model, derives the thermal zones and their envelope from it, and writes a trano configuration. trano turns the configuration into a Modelica model for one of several libraries, which OpenModelica simulates. This page explains each step, the assumptions made on the way and what the generated models contain.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    ifc["IFC files<br/>architecture (+ heating)"] --> parse["ifctrano<br/>spaces, boundaries,<br/>constructions, heating"]
    parse --> yaml["trano configuration<br/>(YAML, ifctrano config)"]
    yaml --> trano["trano<br/>network of components"]
    trano --> mo["Modelica model<br/>Buildings, IDEAS,<br/>AixLib reduced order, ISO 13790"]
    mo --> om["OpenModelica<br/>(Docker)"]
    om --> results["Results<br/>.mat file, report"]

ifctrano create runs the whole chain. ifctrano config stops at the configuration, which can be reviewed and edited before ifctrano from-config builds (and optionally simulates) the model. Both routes produce the same model: the model is always built from the configuration.

docs.title: What is read
docs.text:
IFC entity Use IfcSpace One thermal zone per space. Required: a model without spaces is rejected. IfcWall, IfcSlab, IfcRoof, IfcDoor, IfcWindow Envelope and internal elements of the spaces. IfcPlate Internal elements between two spaces only; plates on the envelope are ignored. IfcBuildingElementPart Parts of a wall or slab, merged into their parent element. IfcMaterialLayerSet (through IfcRelAssociatesMaterial or IfcMaterialLayerSetUsage) Constructions: names and thicknesses of the layers. IfcSIUnit (length) Millimetre models are converted to metres. IFC4 MEP elements (heat generators, pumps, valves, radiators, ports) Heating system, see Systems.

IfcRelSpaceBoundary is not used: space boundaries are rarely present, or reliable, in real models. ifctrano derives them from the geometry instead.

docs.title: Spaces and boundaries
docs.text:
For each space, ifctrano:

  1. computes its oriented bounding box, its floor area (footprint of its shape) and its average height (volume over floor area; the bounding box is used when the shape has no footprint);
  2. finds the building elements within 0.5 m of it (clash_clearance_many of IfcOpenShell's geometry tree);
  3. keeps, for each of them, the common surface between the faces of the space's bounding box and of the element's: its area, its outward normal and its polygon;
  4. replaces building element parts by their parent element, and keeps a single slab or roof where several cover the same surface with the same orientation.

An element whose common surfaces are found with two spaces, facing each other, is an internal element between these spaces: the smaller of the two surfaces is its area. All other boundaries are external.

docs.title: Assumptions and known limitations
docs.text:
• Each IfcSpace is one zone: spaces are not merged into larger zones, and a space with an invalid shape is skipped (and logged).
  • Bounding boxes approximate the geometry: curved or strongly non-convex spaces and elements get approximate areas.
  • Only walls, slabs, roofs, doors and windows bound a space towards the outside; other elements (plates, columns, beams, curtain-wall members as such) are ignored on the envelope.
  • An external boundary exchanges heat with the outdoor air, or with the ground for a floor: unheated neighbouring buildings, crawl spaces or spaces missing from the model are treated as outdoors.
  • Only the thicknesses of the layers come from the IFC model: every material gets the same default thermal properties (conductivity 0.046 W/(m·K), specific heat capacity 940 J/(kg·K), density 80 kg/m³), as IFC models rarely carry them. Edit the material section of the configuration to use real values.

docs.title: Kind of boundary
docs.text: Element Tilt Becomes Wall, door, window wall external wall (doors too), or window Roof ceiling external wall facing up Slab, normal pointing up ceiling external wall facing up Slab, normal pointing down floor floor on ground Element shared by two spaces wall, or floor and ceiling for slabs internal wall between the two zones

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text:
The orientation of a surface is given by its outward normal, measured from the north axis of the model (+y by default, see north_axis). trano and the Modelica libraries use the azimuth of the Buildings library: radians from south, positive towards west.

Facade faces Azimuth (rad) South 0 West π/2 (1.57) North π (3.14) East −π/2 (−1.57)

Vertical surfaces are snapped to the closest of the eight main and intermediate directions. The orientation of roofs and slabs does not change their physics: they are given the azimuth 0.

docs.title: Areas
docs.text:
• Walls are gross facade areas, windows included, as trano expects: trano cuts the windows out of the walls of their orientation.
  • The walls and windows of a space are merged per orientation (one wall and one window area per orientation), with the construction of the first wall.
  • Windows larger than the wall of their orientation (overlapping window boxes on glazed facades) are reduced to 90 % of the wall area. A wall is added where a space has windows without walls.

docs.title: Constructions
docs.text:
• Each IfcMaterialLayerSet becomes a construction named after the layer set (or construction_<id> when unnamed), with one layer per IfcMaterialLayer. Names are made valid Modelica identifiers, and distinct layer sets sharing a name get distinct names.
  • Layers without thickness (membranes, foils) are left out: they add no resistance or capacity to one-dimensional conduction, and trano rejects them. Elements whose layer set has no thick layer get default_construction.
  • Elements without a layer set (no association, IfcMaterialList, constituent sets) get default_construction (0.18 m of the default material); internal elements get default_internal_construction.
  • Windows use a double glazing (3 mm glass, 12.7 mm air, 3 mm glass) with a frame U-value of 1.4 W/(m²·K).

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
Each space is a zone of the chosen library; the envelope, internal walls and windows found above are attached to it.

Library Zone model Envelope Buildings (default) Buildings.ThermalZones.Detailed.MixedAir One-dimensional conduction through each layer, windows with solar transmission, long- and shortwave radiation exchange between surfaces, mixed air volume. IDEAS IDEAS.Buildings.Components.Zone Components per wall, window, slab on ground and internal wall. reduced_order AixLib ThermalZones.ReducedOrder.ThermalZone Envelope lumped into resistance–capacitance elements per orientation. iso_13790 AixLib ThermalZones.ISO13790.Zone5R1C Five resistances and one capacitance (ISO 13790 simple hourly method).

The detailed libraries model each surface; the reduced-order ones are faster and coarser. The library comparison shows how Buildings and IDEAS differ on the same building. Every library is simulated in CI on the two zones model (tests/test_simulation.py).

docs.title: Thermal network and boundary conditions
docs.text:
• Internal walls couple the zones they separate; both sides keep their thermal mass.
  • External walls and roofs exchange heat with the outdoor air and receive solar radiation according to their orientation and tilt; floors on ground sit on the ground, at 10 °C (283.15 K, trano's default) for Buildings and the reduced-order zone, while IDEAS and ISO 13790 model the ground themselves.
  • Weather: trano's default, the Uccle (Belgium) typical year shipped with IDEAS, for every library.
  • Occupancy and infiltration: trano's default occupancy, occupied from 7:00 to 19:00, with the internal gains gain = [35; 70; 30] (radiant, convective, latent) scaled by heat_gain_if_occupied = 1/6/4, and an air change rate of 0.9 1/h.
  • Initial temperature of the zones: 21 °C.

All these values are in the configuration written by ifctrano config, where they can be changed.

docs.title: Systems
docs.text:
Without a heating model, the zones are free-floating: no emission or production system is generated. With heating elements in the architecture file or in federated discipline files (--hvac), ifctrano builds the hydronic system described in the heating tutorial:

IFC trano element Modelica component (Buildings) IfcSpaceHeater (radiator) radiator, lumped per space Buildings.Fluid.HeatExchangers.Radiators.RadiatorEN442_2 Radiator valve valve Buildings.Fluid.Actuators.Valves.TwoWayEqualPercentage IfcPump pump Buildings.Fluid.Movers.Preconfigured.SpeedControlled_y (in a trano wrapper) IfcValve (mixing) three_way_valve Buildings.Fluid.Actuators.Valves.ThreeWayEqualPercentageLinear IfcSensor (temperature) temperature_sensor Buildings.Fluid.Sensors.TemperatureTwoPort IfcBoiler boiler, without_storage or default (with a storage tank) variant Buildings.Fluid.Boilers.BoilerPolynomial (and Buildings.Fluid.Storage.StratifiedEnhanced) Heat pump (IfcUnitaryEquipment recognised as such, or --heat-generator) boiler, air_water_heat_pump or water_water_heat_pump variant Buildings.Fluid.HeatPumps.ModularReversible.AirToWaterTableData or Buildings.Fluid.HeatPumps.EquationFitReversible Radiator not connected to a heat generator radiator, idealbus variant Ideal emitter

Radiators of a space are lumped into one emitter whose nominal power is the sum of their OutputCapacity. Missing data are filled in and logged: radiators and pumps are sized from the design heat load of their spaces (simplified EN 12831), the heat generator from the radiators it serves. The heat generator example compares a boiler and a heat pump on the same house.

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
trano adds a controller to every element that needs one. The controllers generated for a hydronic system are:

Controller Controls How Emission control (one per heated space) Radiator valve PI control of the zone air temperature (ASHRAE Guideline 36 zone control loop) towards a set point switched by a schedule. Collector control (one per circuit) Circulator Pump speed following the most open radiator valve of the circuit; the pump stops when no valve asks for heat (hysteresis). Three-way valve control (one per circuit) Mixing valve Proportional control of the supply temperature measured by the circuit's sensor. Boiler control Heat generator Fires when the rooms ask for heat; off above an outdoor temperature of 15 °C; supply set point 80 °C.

The emission control parameters, with trano's defaults:

Parameter Default Meaning temperature_heating_setpoint 294.15 K (21 °C) Set point during occupied hours temperature_heating_setback 289 K (15.85 °C) Set point outside occupied hours (night setback) schedule 3600*{7, 19} Switching times: occupied from 7:00 to 19:00 controller_gain 5 Gain of the controller

They are set under emission_control.parameters of each space in the configuration; the control example compares the default night setback with a constant set point.

docs.title: Checking the physics
docs.text: tests/physics.py reads the parameters driving the simulation (weather file, zone geometry, envelope areas, orientations and constructions, nominal values of the heating components) from the generated Buildings model. The tests compare them with snapshots, so that a change of ifctrano or trano cannot silently change the physics of the models; every difference with the snapshots of earlier trano versions is listed in tests/test_physics.py with its reason. The examples of the tutorials are simulated in CI for every change.

docs.title: Install ifctrano
docs.text:
ifctrano requires Python 3.11 or 3.12.

pip install ifctrano

Check the installation:

ifctrano --help
ifctrano verify

docs.title: Docker (simulation)
docs.text: ifctrano simulates the generated models with OpenModelica in the official OpenModelica Docker image. Install Docker and keep it running to use --simulate-model. The Modelica libraries are installed in the container at its first start, which needs network access.

docs.title: Graphviz (layout)
docs.text:
trano uses Graphviz to place the components of the generated Modelica models. It is optional, but the diagrams are easier to read with it.

  • Windows: install it from graphviz.org and add its bin folder to the PATH.
  • Linux:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install graphviz

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
ifctrano has four commands:

Command Does ifctrano create MODEL [LIBRARY] Builds the Modelica model of an IFC file, next to it. ifctrano config MODEL Writes the trano configuration (YAML) of an IFC file, to review or edit. ifctrano from-config CONFIG [LIBRARY] Builds the Modelica model of a configuration. ifctrano verify Checks the installation.

LIBRARY is Buildings (default), IDEAS, reduced_order or iso_13790:

ifctrano create /path/to/your.ifc
ifctrano create /path/to/your.ifc IDEAS

Options of create:

Option Does --simulate-model Simulates the model in OpenModelica (Docker) and opens an HTML report of the results. --show-space-boundaries Shows the space boundaries computed from the geometry. --hvac PATH Adds a federated heating model (IFC4 MEP); can be given several times. --heat-generator KIND Kind of heat generator: boiler, air_water_heat_pump, water_water_heat_pump or generic.

config takes the same --hvac, --heat-generator and --show-space-boundaries options, and from-config takes --simulate-model.

docs.title: Control strategies
docs.text:
trano controls every heated room with a PI loop on the air temperature, whose set point a schedule switches between an occupied value and a setback value (see How ifctrano works). By default the rooms are heated to 21 °C from 7:00 to 19:00 and to 15.85 °C at night. The configuration written by ifctrano can be edited to change this; this example compares the default night setback with a constant set point, on ExampleHOM with its heating model.

Write the configuration:

ifctrano config ExampleHOM.ifc --hvac ExampleHOM_heating.ifc

and set the setback temperature to the set point in the emission control of each space:

spaces:
- id: space_living1_v3g
  emissions:
  - radiator:
      id: radiator_space_living1_v3g
      parameters:
        nominal_heating_power_positive_for_heating: 3360.0
  - valve:
      id: valve_space_living1_v3g
      control:
        emission_control:
          id: emission_control_space_living1_v3g
          parameters:
            temperature_heating_setback: 294.15

then build (and simulate) the model from the edited configuration:

ifctrano from-config ExampleHOM.yaml --simulate-model

The other parameters of the emission control are temperature_heating_setpoint (294.15 K), schedule (3600*{7, 19}, the switching times in seconds of the day) and controller_gain (5).

Days 3 to 10 of the year (the first 2 simulated days are a warm-up and are left out).

Case Zone Mean [°C] Minimum [°C] Maximum [°C] Radiator heat [kWh] Peak radiator heat [kW] Heat from the generator [kWh] Gas [kWh] Night setback (default) Living1 18.6 15.0 21.8 125 4.4 148 190 Constant set point Living1 20.9 19.9 22.0 162 1.6 183 228

What to expect. With the night setback, the rooms cool down at night and are heated up again at 7:00, which takes a power peak; with a constant set point the rooms stay at 21 °C and the radiators deliver a steadier, higher heat.

What the simulation shows. Over days 3 to 10, the living room averages 18.6 °C with the night setback (15.0 °C at night) and 20.9 °C with the constant set point (never below 19.9 °C). Keeping the house at 21 °C needs 162 kWh of radiator heat instead of 125 kWh (30 % more) and 229 kWh of gas instead of 190 kWh (21 % more). The peak heat is lower with the constant set point, 1.6 kW instead of 4.4 kW: the night setback saves energy but asks for a morning reheat.

docs.title: Heat generators
docs.text:
IFC has no heat-pump class: heat pumps are usually exported as IfcUnitaryEquipment, which ifctrano recognises from their type, name or classification (see How ifctrano works). When the model does not say which kind of generator it contains, it can be given explicitly. This example heats ExampleHOM with the heating model of the heating tutorial, first with its gas boiler, then with an air-to-water heat pump on the same circuits.

from pathlib import Path

from ifctrano.building import Building
from ifctrano.hvac import HeatingOptions, ProductionKind

building = Building.from_ifc(
    Path("ExampleHOM.ifc"),
    hvac_file_paths=[Path("ExampleHOM_heating.ifc")],
    heating_options=HeatingOptions(heat_generator=ProductionKind.air_water_heat_pump),
)
building.save_model()

or, from the command line:

ifctrano create ExampleHOM.ifc --hvac ExampleHOM_heating.ifc --heat-generator air_water_heat_pump

Everything else (radiators, valves, circulators, mixing valves and their controls) is the same in both models.

Days 3 to 10 of the year (the first 2 simulated days are a warm-up and are left out).

Case Zone Mean [°C] Minimum [°C] Maximum [°C] Radiator heat [kWh] Peak radiator heat [kW] Heat from the generator [kWh] Gas [kWh] Electricity [kWh] Gas boiler Mean of the zones 18.6 15.2 21.8 125 4.4 148 190 Air-to-water heat pump Mean of the zones 18.6 15.2 21.8 125 2.8 124 36

What to expect. Both generators feed the same radiators, controlled to the same set points, so the rooms should be as warm in both cases. The difference is the energy bought: natural gas for the boiler, electricity for the heat pump, which takes most of its heat from the outdoor air.

What the simulation shows. Over days 3 to 10, the rooms are equally warm with both generators (18.6 °C on average, between the 15.85 °C setback and the 21 °C set point) and the radiators deliver the same 125 kWh. The boiler burns 190 kWh of natural gas to produce 148 kWh of heat; the heat pump produces 124 kWh from 36 kWh of electricity, a coefficient of performance of about 3.4 in these January days. The heat pump also loses less heat in the circuits (the generator heat is close to the heat of the radiators) and gives a lower peak at the morning reheat (2.8 kW against 4.4 kW).

docs.title: Heating model
docs.text:
This tutorial shows how ifctrano translates a hydronic heating system modelled in BIM into a trano model. The example combines two federated IFC4 models of the same house: the architecture model ExampleHOM.ifc and a heating discipline model sharing its project, site, building and storeys.

The heating model follows common IFC4 MEP practice: a gas condensing boiler (IfcBoiler), two heating circuits (ground floor and first floor), each with a circulator (IfcPump), a three-way mixing valve (IfcValve, MIXING) and a flow temperature sensor (IfcSensor), and eleven panel radiators (IfcSpaceHeater, RADIATOR) with thermostatic radiator valves. Elements are connected with pipe segments and fittings through IfcDistributionPorts, grouped in supply and return IfcDistributionSystems, and typed with the standard property sets (Pset_SpaceHeaterTypeCommon.OutputCapacity, Pset_BoilerTypeWater.HeatOutput, Pset_PumpTypeCommon.FlowRateRange, ...).

The heating network on its own, with supply pipes in red and return pipes in blue. The boiler, circulators (green) and mixing valves (purple) are in the kitchen; the radiators (orange) are placed in the rooms.

The heating model is generated by tests/hvac/example_hom_heating.py and can be written to a file with:

python -m tests.hvac.example_hom_heating ExampleHOM_heating.ifc

docs.title: Generate the model
docs.text:
The heating model is passed next to the architecture model:

ifctrano create ExampleHOM.ifc Buildings --hvac ExampleHOM_heating.ifc

or with Python:

from pathlib import Path

from ifctrano.building import Building

building = Building.from_ifc(
    Path("ExampleHOM.ifc"), hvac_file_paths=[Path("ExampleHOM_heating.ifc")]
)
building.save_model(library="Buildings")

Heating elements contained in the architecture file itself are also taken into account, so single-file models work without --hvac.

docs.title: What ifctrano does
docs.text:
1. Network: the port connections are turned into a directed graph. Pipes, fittings, isolating valves and sensors only carry connectivity; heat generators, circulators, mixing valves and radiators are the active components.
  2. Spaces: each radiator is assigned to the space it is referenced in (IfcRelReferencedInSpatialStructure, matched by GlobalId across the federated models) or, when the model has no such relation, to the space whose footprint contains it.
  3. Circuits: radiators fed by the same heat generator through the same circulator and mixing valve form a circuit. Each circuit becomes trano's hydronic circuit: pump, three-way valve, temperature sensor, radiators with their valves, and a collector returning to the boiler.
  4. Parameters: the radiators of a space are lumped into one emitter whose nominal power is the sum of their OutputCapacity (the living room has two 1680 W radiators). The boiler power comes from HeatOutput and the pump nominal flow and head from FlowRateRange and FlowResistanceRange.

The resulting hydronic model, as generated by trano, is shown below. Supply connections are in red, return connections in blue, and the dashed lines are the bypasses of the three-way valves.

The same information is available in the configuration generated by ifctrano config ExampleHOM.ifc --hvac ExampleHOM_heating.ifc. Each heated space gets its emission:

spaces:
- id: space_living1_v3g
  emissions:
  - radiator:
      id: radiator_space_living1_v3g
      parameters:
        nominal_heating_power_positive_for_heating: 3360.0
  - valve:
      id: valve_space_living1_v3g
      control:
        emission_control:
          id: emission_control_space_living1_v3g

and the boiler and circuits are described in the systems section (ground floor circuit shown):

systems:
- boiler:
    id: boiler_1
    variant: without_storage
    control:
      boiler_control:
        id: boiler_control_boiler_1
    parameters:
      nominal_heating_power: 18000.0
    inlets:
    - split_valve_1
    - split_valve_2
- pump:
    id: pump_1
    control:
      collector_control:
        id: collector_control_pump_1
    parameters:
      dp_nominal: 40000.0
      m_flow_nominal: 0.25
    inlets:
    - boiler_1
- three_way_valve:
    id: three_way_valve_1
    control:
      three_way_valve_control:
        id: three_way_valve_control_1
    inlets:
    - split_valve_1
    - pump_1
    outlets:
    - temperature_sensor_1
- temperature_sensor:
    id: temperature_sensor_1
    outlets:
    - radiator_space_corridor3_n2a
    - radiator_space_hobby2_uxa
    - radiator_space_kitchen5_dsw
    - radiator_space_living1_v3g
    - radiator_space_wc4_pwg
- split_valve:
    id: split_valve_1
    inlets:
    - valve_space_corridor3_n2a
    - valve_space_hobby2_uxa
    - valve_space_kitchen5_dsw
    - valve_space_living1_v3g
    - valve_space_wc4_pwg
    outlets:
    - boiler_1

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The model simulated for the first ten days of January in Uccle (trano's default weather), with trano's default controls: the rooms are heated to 21 °C from 7:00 to 19:00 and to 15.85 °C at night (see Control). The second panel shows the heat delivered by all the radiators.

Days 3 to 10 of the year (the first 2 simulated days are a warm-up and are left out).

Case Zone Mean [°C] Minimum [°C] Maximum [°C] Radiator heat [kWh] Peak radiator heat [kW] Heat from the generator [kWh] Gas [kWh] Gas boiler Att 13.0 9.1 18.3 Gas boiler Bath9 19.6 15.4 25.6 Gas boiler Bedroom6 19.1 15.4 21.7 Gas boiler Children10 19.6 15.4 24.2 Gas boiler Children7 18.6 14.9 21.4 Gas boiler Corridor3 19.7 16.3 21.7 Gas boiler Corridor8 20.0 16.5 22.3 Gas boiler Hobby2 18.9 15.5 21.4 Gas boiler Kitchen5 18.8 15.1 24.2 Gas boiler Living1 18.6 15.0 21.8 Gas boiler Wc4 18.9 15.5 21.7 Gas boiler Mean of the zones 18.6 15.2 21.8 125 4.4 148 190

What to expect. The heated rooms follow the schedule of their emission control: they are brought to about 21 °C during the day and cool down towards the 15.85 °C setback at night. The radiators deliver most of their heat when the set point switches back to 21 °C in the morning. The attic has no radiator and floats.

What the simulation shows. Over days 3 to 10, the heated rooms average 18.6 to 20 °C, between their day set point and their night setback; their minima (15 to 16.5 °C) are the night setback and their maxima (21.4 to 22.3 °C) the day set point, with sunny rooms going above it (up to about 25 °C in the bathroom, kitchen and children's room 10, which have south windows). The unheated attic averages 13 °C. The radiators deliver 125 kWh over the eight days, with a peak of 4.4 kW (hourly mean) when the rooms are heated up after the night setback (see the control example). The boiler produces 148 kWh, so about 23 kWh are lost in the distribution circuits, and burns 190 kWh of natural gas (lower heating value): a seasonal efficiency of about 78 %.

Difference with earlier versions. With trano 0.39 (ifctrano 0.15), the rooms were heated to 23.85 °C during the day, the model read the Chicago weather file, and the boiler kept its water hot day and night with a casing loss that trano 0.42 corrected. trano 0.42 heats to 21 °C, reads the Uccle weather and fires the boiler on demand, so the heat demand and the gas use are lower than they were.

docs.title: Incomplete models
docs.text:
Real models often lack part of this information. ifctrano keeps going and records every assumption, which is logged and available in building.heating.assumptions:

  • Flow directions: exporters draw some pipes against the flow. ifctrano follows the modelled direction where it can, crosses wrongly drawn segments when it must (as few as possible), and only accepts a route from the heat generator to a radiator through a circulator, since no flow reaches a radiator otherwise.
  • Sizing: when radiators have no OutputCapacity, each space's emitter is sized for the design heat load of the space, computed with a simplified EN 12831-1 method from its external boundaries (transmission through walls, roofs, windows, and floors on ground) and its ventilation. Pumps without FlowRateRange get the flow carrying the power of the radiators they serve between the design supply and return temperatures, and the boiler power defaults to the sum of the radiators it serves.
  • Heat generators: neither IFC4 nor IFC4.3 has a heat-pump class. Heat pumps exported as IfcUnitaryEquipment are recognised from ObjectType="HEATPUMP", their (type) name, model label or classification; otherwise they are modelled as a boiler. Their kind can also be given explicitly.
  • Unconnected radiators become ideal emitters, and a circuit without its own circulator or mixing valve gets the default ones of trano's circuit template.

The design conditions and the kind of heat generator are set with HeatingOptions:

from pathlib import Path

from ifctrano.building import Building
from ifctrano.hvac import DesignConditions, HeatingOptions, ProductionKind

building = Building.from_ifc(
    Path("architecture.ifc"),
    hvac_file_paths=[Path("heating.ifc")],
    heating_options=HeatingOptions(
        heat_generator=ProductionKind.water_water_heat_pump,
        design=DesignConditions(outdoor_temperature=-12.0, supply_temperature=45.0, return_temperature=35.0),
    ),
)

or, for the kind of heat generator, from the command line:

ifctrano create architecture.ifc --hvac heating.ifc --heat-generator water_water_heat_pump

The figures of this page are generated by docs_src/heating_figures.py.

docs.title: Many zones model
docs.text:
ifctrano makes one thermal zone per IfcSpace, and couples the zones through the walls and slabs they share. This tutorial uses MultiZoneBuilding.ifc from tests/models/space_boundary.

from pathlib import Path

from ifctrano.building import Building

building = Building.from_ifc(Path("MultiZoneBuilding.ifc"))
building.save_model()

or, showing the space boundaries and simulating the model:

ifctrano create MultiZoneBuilding.ifc --show-space-boundaries --simulate-model

The space boundaries derived from the geometry: external surfaces in red, surfaces shared between spaces in blue.

The generated model in OpenModelica (taken with an earlier version; the layout may differ):

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The building has no heating model: the zones are free-floating. With more zones than lines can show clearly, the figure draws the range of the zone temperatures (minimum to maximum) and their mean.

Days 3 to 10 of the year (the first 2 simulated days are a warm-up and are left out).

Case Zone Mean [°C] Minimum [°C] Maximum [°C] Multizone 01 8.5 4.6 15.8 Multizone 1yy 8.9 5.6 16.3 Multizone 8z 7.6 3.8 17.1 Multizone Ah1 10.0 7.1 14.2 Multizone Av0 9.2 5.8 16.5 Multizone Bll 9.2 5.8 16.5 Multizone Dn 9.2 5.8 16.5 Multizone H8c 9.1 5.9 16.3 Multizone Kjt 9.2 5.8 16.5 Multizone Pmi 6.9 2.9 15.3 Multizone Uh1 9.3 5.8 16.5 Multizone Uso 9.3 5.8 16.5 Multizone V1e 7.3 4.0 13.0 Multizone Mean of the zones 8.7 5.3 14.7

What to expect. The zones are coupled through the internal walls, so their temperatures follow each other; the zones with more external surface (and less internal gain per volume) are colder.

What the simulation shows. The thirteen zones stay between 3 and 17 °C, with a mean of about 9 °C over days 3 to 10. The spread between the zones (about 3 K on the mean temperature, from 6.9 °C to 10.0 °C) comes from their exposure: the six identical rooms with 8 m² of external wall and a 4 m² window all average 9.2 to 9.3 °C, while the two zones with the most external wall (45 m² and 29 m²) and no window are the coldest (6.9 °C and 7.3 °C).

docs.title: Orientation of the facades
docs.text:
The orientation of every wall and window comes from the geometry: ifctrano measures the outward normal of each surface from the north axis of the model (+y by default) and converts it to the azimuth of the Modelica libraries (see How ifctrano works). This example shows its effect on the simulated temperatures: the same house, without heating, as built and turned by 180°.

The kitchen of ExampleHOM has windows on its south and west facades. Turning the north axis by 180° makes them face north and east.

from pathlib import Path

from ifctrano.base import Vector
from ifctrano.building import Building

building = Building.from_ifc(Path("ExampleHOM.ifc"))
as_built = building.to_config()
turned = building.to_config(north_axis=Vector(x=0, y=-1, z=0))

north_axis is the direction of north in the coordinates of the model: Vector(x=0, y=-1, z=0) puts north along -y. Both configurations are simulated from 21 March, when the sun is low enough for the facades to make a difference, in the Uccle weather.

Days 83 to 90 of the year (the first 2 simulated days are a warm-up and are left out).

Case Zone Mean [°C] Minimum [°C] Maximum [°C] As built (kitchen windows south and west) Kitchen5 24.8 15.2 39.4 Turned by 180° (north and east) Kitchen5 22.7 13.8 32.1

What to expect. In late March the sun is low in the south during the day and sets in the west: a room with south and west windows gets much more solar gain than the same room facing north and east, which only sees the morning sun on its east window.

What the simulation shows. As built, the kitchen averages 24.8 °C over days 83 to 90, peaking at about 39 °C in the afternoons. Turned by 180°, it averages 22.7 °C (2.1 K less) and peaks at about 32 °C. The night minima differ less (15.2 °C and 13.8 °C): the difference is the solar gain of the day. The peaks are high because the house has no heating, no shading and no thermal mass (the default materials, see the limitations).

Difference with earlier versions. Before ifctrano 0.15 the azimuths were turned by 180°: the "as built" case of this page was then simulated as the "turned" one.

docs.title: Realistic model
docs.text:
This tutorial uses a realistic BIM model: the duplex apartment sample model, a two-storey dwelling with many rooms (Duplex_A.ifc in tests/models/space_boundary).

from pathlib import Path

from ifctrano.building import Building

building = Building.from_ifc(Path("Duplex_A.ifc"))
building.save_model()

or

ifctrano create Duplex_A.ifc --show-space-boundaries --simulate-model

The space boundaries derived from the geometry:

The generated model in OpenModelica (taken with an earlier version; the layout may differ):

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Free-floating zones (the model has no heating) for the first ten days of January.

Days 3 to 10 of the year (the first 2 simulated days are a warm-up and are left out).

Case Zone Mean [°C] Minimum [°C] Maximum [°C] Duplex A101 12.2 9.9 15.3 Duplex A102 13.4 6.0 42.9 Duplex A103 11.5 9.3 14.6 Duplex A104 10.7 9.5 12.0 Duplex A105 11.0 9.4 13.2 Duplex A201 12.8 10.6 15.7 Duplex A202 11.1 7.4 19.9 Duplex A203 12.2 8.4 26.9 Duplex A204 12.5 10.5 15.2 Duplex A205 12.3 10.2 14.8 Duplex B101 3q 11.0 9.3 12.8 Duplex B102 cz 8.6 5.2 13.2 Duplex B103 3s 11.8 9.4 14.7 Duplex B104 3p 10.5 9.4 11.8 Duplex B105 10.6 9.0 12.5 Duplex B201 3g 13.0 11.2 15.3 Duplex B202 3a 10.6 8.5 15.8 Duplex B203 39 9.9 7.1 14.1 Duplex B204 3c 12.4 10.5 14.7 Duplex B205 12.1 10.4 14.3 Duplex R301 20.4 14.6 26.7 Duplex Mean of the zones 11.9 9.4 15.8

What to expect. Most rooms stay between the outdoor temperature and 15 °C without heating; rooms with large windows and little floor area heat up in the sun.

What the simulation shows. The mean of the 21 zones is 12 °C over days 3 to 10, most rooms averaging between 10 and 13.5 °C. Two rooms stand out:

  • A102 averages 13 °C but peaks at about 43 °C on sunny afternoons. It has 11.7 m² of windows for 27.7 m² of floor, and, like every room, constructions made of ifctrano's default material, an insulation-like material of 80 kg/m³ (see the limitations): almost no thermal mass absorbs the solar gains. Such peaks in January are an artefact of the default material properties.
  • The roof space R301 averages 20 °C: no roof surface was found for it (only 31.6 m² of external wall for 135 m² of floor), so the internal gains of its large floor area have little surface to escape through.

Edit the material section of the configuration with the real properties of the materials, and check the space boundaries (--show-space-boundaries), before drawing conclusions on overheating.

docs.title: Two zones model
docs.text: This tutorial generates the Modelica model of a small building with two spaces, simulates it and reads the results. The IFC file, TwoZones.ifc, is in tests/models/space_boundary of the repository.

docs.title: Generate the model
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

from ifctrano.building import Building

building = Building.from_ifc(Path("TwoZones.ifc"))
building.show()  # space boundaries computed from the geometry
building.save_model()  # TwoZones.mo next to the IFC file, for the Buildings library

building.show() displays the space boundaries ifctrano derived from the geometry: the surfaces each space shares with the walls, slabs, roof and windows around it, and with the other space.

The same from the command line (ifctrano create --help lists the options):

ifctrano create TwoZones.ifc --show-space-boundaries

The model opens in OpenModelica (or Dymola) once the Buildings library is loaded. The diagram below was taken with an earlier version; the layout of the components may differ.

docs.title: Simulate
docs.text:
With Docker running, --simulate-model simulates the model in OpenModelica and opens an HTML report of the results:

ifctrano create TwoZones.ifc --simulate-model

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The building has no heating model, so the zones are free-floating: their temperature results from the losses through the envelope, the solar gains through the windows and the internal gains of the occupants. The figure shows the first ten days of January in Uccle (trano's default weather).

Days 3 to 10 of the year (the first 2 simulated days are a warm-up and are left out).

Case Zone Mean [°C] Minimum [°C] Maximum [°C] Two zones 01 (dup) 8.1 5.8 11.3 Two zones 01 (uj9) 9.7 6.1 17.3 Two zones Mean of the zones 8.9 6.0 13.9

What to expect. Without heating, the zones settle between the outdoor temperature (dotted line) and the comfort range: the envelope loses heat to the outdoor air, while the occupants and the sun bring heat in. Only zone 01 (uj9) has a window (1 m²), so it warms up more on sunny days.

What the simulation shows. Over days 3 to 10, the mean air temperature of the zones is about 9 °C. The zone with the window averages 9.7 °C and reaches about 17 °C on sunny afternoons; the other averages 8.1 °C and stays within 6 to 11 °C. Both stay well above the outdoor temperature: the default constructions are very insulating (see the limitations).

docs.title: Use different libraries
docs.text:
ifctrano generates models for four Modelica libraries:

LIBRARY Library Zone model Buildings (default) Buildings Detailed: every surface, layer and window IDEAS IDEAS Detailed: every surface, layer and window reduced_order AixLib Reduced order: resistance–capacitance network iso_13790 AixLib ISO 13790 5R1C simple hourly method

The library is given to save_model:

from pathlib import Path

from ifctrano.building import Building

building = Building.from_ifc(Path("TwoZones.ifc"))
building.save_model(library="IDEAS")

or as the second argument of ifctrano create:

ifctrano create TwoZones.ifc IDEAS

The IDEAS model of the two zones, as opened in OpenModelica (taken with an earlier version; the layout may differ):

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The same configuration of the two zones model simulated with Buildings and IDEAS, for the first ten days of January, without heating. The figure shows the mean air temperature of the two zones.

AixLib models

The reduced_order and iso_13790 models simulate with --simulate-model since trano 0.43.0, which loads AixLib and installs it in the OpenModelica container. CI simulates the two zones model in all four libraries (tests/test_simulation.py); this comparison shows the two detailed libraries.

Days 3 to 10 of the year (the first 2 simulated days are a warm-up and are left out).

Case Zone Mean [°C] Minimum [°C] Maximum [°C] Buildings Mean of the zones 8.9 6.0 13.9 IDEAS Mean of the zones 8.8 5.8 13.8

What to expect. Both libraries describe each wall, window and floor with the same constructions, so free-floating temperatures should be close; differences come from the models of the convection, the radiation exchange, the windows and the ground.

What the simulation shows. Over days 3 to 10, the mean temperature of the zones is 8.9 °C with Buildings and 8.8 °C with IDEAS, with minima of 6.0 and 5.8 °C and maxima of 13.9 and 13.8 °C: the two detailed libraries agree within 0.2 K on this building.
